paper_title: Ensemble Routing for Prompt-Adaptive Cost-Aware LLM Inference

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support Web-based services that must balance response quality and inference cost across heterogeneous requests. Conventional routing selects one model per prompt, while fixed ensembles cannot adapt their composition and cost to individual requests. We introduce PISA, a prompt-adaptive, cost-aware single-model router, and PISA-E, its extension to ensemble routing. At the core of both methods, PISA combines soft cluster memberships with model-specific predictors to estimate individual model capabilities. Building on these estimates, PISA-E jointly selects ensemble composition and cardinality under an explicit cost--quality preference that can be adjusted at inference time without retraining. A tractable ensemble-success surrogate and efficient candidate selection enable this extension without ensemble-specific training. Across four LLM routing benchmarks under in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions, PISA achieves the highest macro-average cost--performance hypervolume among the evaluated single-model routers in both settings. Meanwhile, PISA-E achieves the highest macro-average task performance among the evaluated ensemble approaches when prioritizing response quality, surpassing the strongest competitors by 2.09 and 2.87 percentage points under ID and OOD conditions, respectively. At selected lower-cost operating points, it also exceeds the strongest ensemble competitors' macro-average task performance while reducing average inference cost by approximately 36% and 25%, respectively. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of prompt-adaptive capability estimation for both single-model routing and selective ensembling.

sections.title:
1 Introduction
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in Web-
based services, supporting applications such as search and infor-
mation discovery, recommendation, and intelligent agents [3, 16].
Their adoption also extends to publicly accessible LLM services, cre-
ating new challenges for efficient and scalable inference [22]. These
services must handle heterogeneous user requests while balancing
response quality and inference cost. When multiple LLMs with
different capabilities and pricing structures are available, invoking
expensive models indiscriminately wastes resources, whereas con-
sistently selecting inexpensive models can compromise response
quality. Moreover, different users and requests may have different
sections.content: cost preferences, making it desirable to adapt inference strategies to both prompt characteristics and inference-cost preferences [31]. LLM routing addresses this challenge by selecting models according to prompt characteristics, expected response quality, and inference cost [25]. Recent approaches extend routing to budget-adaptive selection [43], reasoning-strategy selection [26], and additional deployment constraints [20]. However, selecting single model cannot exploit the complementary capabilities of multiple LLMs. Ensembling offers an alternative by combining multiple model responses [5], but introduces additional inference costs. Existing ensemble approaches explore adaptive model composition, diversityaware selection, and budget-constrained optimization [6, 15, 30]. Nevertheless, existing approaches typically address only parts of the problem: some adapt ensemble composition without explicitly optimizing inference cost, while others rely on classification-specific aggregation or sequential execution. Moreover, ensemble cardinality is generally fixed during training or configuration, limiting the ability to adjust the number of invoked models to individual prompts and changing cost preferences at inference time. This motivates ensemble routing, where both the composition and cardinality of the invoked model subset are determined dynamically at inference time according to prompt characteristics and an explicit costquality preference. We introduce PISA, prompt-adaptive, cost-aware single-model router that estimates the capabilities of individual LLMs, and PISA-E, its extension to prompt-adaptive ensemble routing. PISA-E reuses the individual capability estimates to construct tractable surrogate for ensemble success, eliminating the need to train separate quality estimators for different model combinations. By combining these estimates with inference cost, PISA-E selects prompt-specific model subsets, jointly determining which models to invoke and how many. Crucially, the costquality preference can be adjusted at inference time without additional hyperparameter optimization or retraining, allowing the same framework to support different operating points. The selected responses are combined through capability-weighted semantic similarity to produce the final ensemble response. We evaluate PISA and PISA-E on four LLM routing benchmarks under in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions. PISA achieves the highest macro-average hypervolume among the evaluated single-model routers in both settings, ranking first in six of the eight benchmarksetting combinations. PISA-E achieves the highest macro-average task performance among the evaluated ensemble approaches in both settings, improving over the strongest competitors by 2.09 percentage points under ID and 2.87 under OOD conditions when prioritizing response quality. At selected lowercost operating points, it also exceeds the strongest competitors macro-average task performance while reducing average inference cost by approximately 36% and 25%, respectively. Finally, comparisons with fixed-cardinality variants demonstrate the benefits of adapting ensemble size to individual prompts. Our main contributions are: We develop PISA, prompt-adaptive, cost-aware singlemodel router that estimates individual model capabilities through soft cluster memberships and model-specific predictors, providing the foundation for ensemble routing. We propose PISA-E, framework for prompt-adaptive, cost-aware ensemble routing that uses ensemble-level utility estimates derived from individual model capabilities to jointly determine ensemble composition and cardinality at inference time, according to prompt characteristics and inference-cost preferences. We evaluate both methods across four benchmarks under ID and OOD conditions, demonstrating the highest macroaverage single-model routing HV and ensemble task performance among the evaluated approaches in both settings. We also demonstrate operating points with higher task performance at lower cost than the strongest ensemble competitors and quantify the benefits of prompt-dependent ranking and adaptive ensemble cardinality.

sections.title:
4 Experiments
4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Benchmarks. We evaluate PISA and PISA-E on four LLM routing benchmarks: LLMRouterBench Track-2 [19], RouterBench [13], FusionBench [10], and SPROUT [27]. These benchmarks cover heterogeneous candidate model pools and task groups, with performance measured using their respective evaluation scores. Ensemble Routing for Prompt-Adaptive Cost-Aware LLM Inference Evaluation Protocol. We consider both ID and OOD evaluations. For ID experiments, we use the released data partitions when available; otherwise, we split the data into 70% development and 30% test, further dividing the development set into 80% training and 20% validation. For OOD experiments, we train exclusively on ID task groups, select configurations using ID validation data, and evaluate on held-out task groups. ID and OOD experiments use separately fitted routers. All experiments are evaluated over five seeds, with fixed data partitions, and all approaches are evaluated using the model responses provided by the benchmarks. Baselines. We compare PISA against four single-model routing baselines: EmbedLLM [41], Avengers-Pro [37, 38], K-NN, and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). For PISA-E, we consider five LLM ensembling approaches: DFPE [6], LLM-TOPLA [30], SelectLLM [24], PairRanker [17], and BERTScore-based MBR [36]. PairRanker employs PairRM, the pairwise reward model introduced by LLMBlender, to rank candidate responses. We evaluate its pretrained checkpoint (PairRanker-PT) and fine-tuned variant (PairRankerFT), trained following the original procedure. We additionally report an oracle single-model selector that uses ground-truth evaluation scores to select the best-performing model for each prompt, providing reference for the performance attainable through perfect model selection. Metrics. We report task performance and inference cost, computed from benchmark-specific scores and model invocation costs. Task performance is macro-averaged across task groups. To summarize costperformance trade-offs, we use normalized dominated hypervolume (HV), multiplied by 100. The reference performance corresponds to random router, while the reference cost is set to the 40th percentile of the full-pool cost distribution for single-model routing and the 70th percentile for ensemble routing. These reference points are chosen to accommodate all the operating points of the compared methods. Since existing ensemble approaches generally provide single operating point rather than costperformance frontier, we compare them directly in terms of task performance and inference cost. Implementation. We employ Qwen3-Embedding-8B [39] for creating the prompt embeddings required by the routers. PISA-E considers ensembles of up to eleven models. Hyperparameters and ensemble configurations are selected independently for each benchmark using validation task performance at 𝛼 = 1. The same fitted capability estimators are reused across different costperformance operating points. Further implementation details, including the HV definition, are provided in Appendix A.

Table 6 reports task performance at 𝛼 = 1 under ID and OOD conditions. GC improves performance for several resolver configurations, particularly other-weighted BERTScore and PairRanker. However, these improvements do not consistently extend to self-weighted BERTScore, for which PB achieves higher macro-average performance in both ID (75.27% versus 75.23%) and OOD (63.24% versus 62.36%) settings. Overall, PB combined with self-weighted BERTScore achieves the highest aggregate performance, indicating that explicitly modeling correctness dependencies does not consistently improve ensemble performance and supporting the simpler PB formulation as the default estimator. Ensemble Resolver Quality. We further investigate how the choice of response resolver affects ensemble performance. As shown in Table 6, self-weighted BERTScore achieves the highest aggregate performance among the evaluated resolvers when paired with PB, outperforming standard BERTScore by 0.92 percentage points in ID and 1.21 percentage points in OOD settings. In contrast, PairRanker exhibits greater sensitivity to the ensemble-success estimator, with GC substantially improving performance over PB for both pretrained and fine-tuned variants. Fine-tuning consistently improves PairRanker performance over its pretrained counterpart under both estimation methods, although neither variant surpasses self-weighted BERTScore in aggregate performance. These findings support capability-weighted semantic similarity as an effective response resolution strategy and motivate self-weighted BERTScore as the default resolver in PISA-E. sections.title: Ranking
sections.content: To assess the contribution of prompt-dependent model ranking, we compare PISA-E against fixed-global baseline that retains adaptive ensemble cardinality but ranks models using their global training-set capabilities instead of prompt-specific estimates. This isolates the effect of prompt-dependent ranking while preserving the cost-aware ensemble selection framework. Table 7 shows that PISA-E improves macro-average HV by 4.96 points under ID conditions and 0.91 points under OOD conditions. It outperforms the fixed-global baseline on all four ID benchmarks and on Track-2 and RouterBench under OOD conditions, while the baseline performs better on FusionBench and SPROUT. Across all eight scenarios, PISA-E achieves macro-average HV of 32.82 compared with 29.89 for the fixed-global baseline, indicating that promptdependent ranking contributes to costperformance improvements independently of adaptive cardinality.

sections.title: 5 Related Work
sections.content: Cost-Aware Model Routing. LLM routing selects model for each prompt by estimating response quality and accounting for inference cost. EmbedLLM [41] learns latent representations from modelquestion correctness matrix. Clustering-based methods instead use similarities among prompts to estimate model performance: UniRoute [18] and Avengers-PRO [37, 38] rely on hard cluster assignments and cluster-level statistics, while ZeroRouter [35] combines clustering with item response theory. PISA differs in using soft cluster memberships and model-specific predictors to estimate prompt-dependent capabilities. Related cost-aware inference strategies include LLM cascades [4, 8] and risk-aware routing [12]. Cascades may escalate requests sequentially; PISA-E instead selects models for parallel execution before generating their responses. LLM Ensembling and Response Aggregation. LLM ensembling combines responses from multiple models to exploit complementary capabilities. Aggregation methods include majority voting [1, 33], learned ranking and fusion, as in LLM-Blender [17] and URG [23], Urso et al. and similarity-based minimum Bayes risk decoding, including variants that account for uncertainty [7]. Multi-agent debate [9] and Mixture-of-Agents [32] also combine model outputs, but involve interaction across successive rounds or stages. PISA-E does not organize such collaboration: after selecting an ensemble, it queries the models in parallel and resolves their responses using capabilityweighted semantic similarity. Adaptive and Cost-Aware Ensemble Selection. Ensemble selection determines which models to invoke, and whether that choice changes across queries. LLM-TOPLA [30] and DFPE [6] construct ensembles that are subsequently reused across queries, whereas SelectLLM [24] adapts ensemble composition to the input while retaining fixed cardinality. ThriftLLM [14] jointly adapts composition and cardinality under cost constraints, but addresses classification queries rather than open-ended response generation. Other adaptive multi-model approaches make different inference decisions. EMS [21] expands the set of invoked models sequentially; LightRouter [40] combines model selection with staged collaboration; and retrieval-based selection and response enhancement are investigated in [29]. Query-specific agentic systems instead configure task plans, agents, or collaboration strategies [11, 28, 34]. PISA-E targets pre-inference selection of parallel ensemble for response generation. It scores candidate subsets using strict-majority surrogate constructed from prompt-dependent individual capability estimates, jointly selecting composition and cardinality under an explicit costquality preference without training ensemble-specific predictors.

sections.title:
6 Conclusion
We introduced PISA, a prompt-adaptive, cost-aware single-model
router, and PISA-E, its extension to ensemble routing. Both methods
use prompt-dependent capability estimates, which PISA-E reuses
to jointly select ensemble composition and cardinality without
ensemble-specific training. Across four heterogeneous benchmarks,
PISA achieves the highest macro-average hypervolume among
the evaluated single-model routers under both ID and OOD con-
ditions. PISA-E achieves the highest macro-average task perfor-
mance among the evaluated ensemble approaches, exceeding the
strongest competitors by 2.09 and 2.87 percentage points, respec-
tively, when prioritizing response quality. At selected lower-cost
operating points, PISA-E also improves macro-average task per-
formance while reducing average inference cost by approximately
36% under ID and 25% under OOD conditions. Component anal-
yses and ablations support the contributions of capability-aware
response resolution, prompt-dependent ranking, and adaptive en-
semble cardinality. Together, these results demonstrate that a shared
capability-estimation framework supports effective single-model
routing and selective ensembling, with cost–quality preferences
adjustable at inference time without retraining. For Web-based ser-
vices such as search, recommendation, and intelligent agents, this
flexibility offers a way to adapt inference expenditure to heteroge-
neous user requests and changing quality–cost preferences.

sections.content: Benchmarks and evaluation scores. Table 8 summarizes the evaluated benchmarks. We use the original evaluation scores provided by each benchmark, which are all in the range [0, 1]. FusionBench uses binary correctness, SPROUT employs LLM-judge scores, while RouterBench and Track-2 include task-dependent evaluation scores. Task performance is computed by averaging scores within each task group and then taking the macro-average across groups, consistently for all methods. For capability estimation, PISA derives binary success labels from the training scores using 𝑦𝑖𝑚 = 1[𝑠𝑖𝑚 0.5] and trains model-specific predictors on these labels. Entire task groups are assigned either to ID, which supplies training and validation data, or to OOD, which is reserved exclusively for testing. All available rows of held-out groups are used for OOD evaluation, irrespective of their original partition. The group assignments are selected without considering model outcomes, targeting approximately 20% of the available prompts for OOD evaluation, subject to 30% upper bound. We require at least three OOD groups spanning three task categories and domains, and at least three retained ID groups. Among valid partitions, we select those closest to the target proportion. Thus, reported standard deviations measure run-to-run variability under fixed data partitions. Baselines. DFPE follows its clustering and representative selection procedure, using global statistics fitted on ID training data when evaluating held-out OOD task groups. sections.title: Cardinality
sections.content: Table 10 examines the effect of restricting the maximum ensemble cardinality 𝑘max. Under ID conditions, PISA-E achieves macroaverage HV of 39.35 with 𝑘max = 11, remaining competitive when the maximum cardinality is reduced, with HV reaching 39.41 at 𝑘max = 7. Under OOD conditions, allowing larger ensembles provides more substantial benefits, although restricting 𝑘max to seven still yields an HV of 26.07, compared with 26.30 when allowing up to eleven models. Thus, PISA-E retains strong aggregate cost performance trade-offs under moderate restrictions on ensemble cardinality, while the larger gains observed under OOD conditions highlight the benefits of access to broader range of ensemble sizes.
